# From model to service {#sec-ch14}

::: {.epigraph by="A saying among site reliability engineers"}
Hope is not a strategy.
:::

Every project reaches the moment when the prototype works and someone asks: "Can we run it on Monday?" A model that decides well on a laptop is not a service. A service answers at 3 a.m. when the API is slow, explains itself to an auditor a year later, tells someone when the world has changed, and changes safely when you improve it. This chapter covers what that takes, and ends by building a small System One model of your own.

::: {.goals}
- Call a model you don't own safely: versions, retries, failures.
- Make every decision explainable with a record.
- See what's inside a small System One model.
:::

## Calling a model you don't own

**Build against a stand-in, then flip one switch.** The official library builds requests, retries failures and parses answers; only its last layer, the *transport*, talks to the network, and you can swap it. The book's stand-in plugs in there, so your code runs exactly as it would for real, for free. Then go live by changing one setting.

![The official library does all the work of building requests, retrying and parsing answers. The transport decides where requests go. The book's stand-in answers locally; the default sends them over the network to TypeSafe.](/figures/ch23/layers.pdf){#fig-layers}

**Pin the model version.** A name like "latest" can point to a new model at any time.

::: {.keyidea}
Fix the model version, so a change in behaviour is your decision, not a surprise.
:::

**Retry the right errors.** Your own mistakes (no key, a model name that doesn't exist) fail the same way every time: fix them. Problems outside your code (rate limits, server errors, dropped connections) are worth retrying. If one request in five fails, only {{< num ch23 ok_20_0 pct >}} of calls succeed with no retries and {{< num ch23 ok_20_2 pct1 >}} with two. But retries cost time, and a login check may have only 300 milliseconds.

**Decide what failure means.** So treat a failed call as just another case the policy must handle. For a login, "allow, but flag for review" may be right; for closing an alert, "don't close, send to a person". Put that rule in the policy where people can see it.

::: {.keyidea}
When time matters, decide in advance what a failed call means.
:::

**Ask together, and test for free.** Four questions in one call used about {{< num ch23 tokens_four_one int >}} input tokens; in four calls, {{< num ch23 tokens_four_sep int >}}. And record real answers once, then replay them in every test run, so tests cost nothing and a changed question fails loudly.

## The service

![The decision service. Each alert's trusted fields go to Jev as three typed questions; the answer is calibrated, and the policy, business rules and capacity turn it into a zone. Every decision is recorded before it is returned. Any failure falls back to review. A daily monitor reads the log, and a candidate version can run in shadow beside the current one.](/figures/ch28/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-21}

You'll recognise every box in @fig-architecture-21. What turns a chain of steps into a service is four habits.

**One configuration, one fingerprint.** The model version, calibration numbers, thresholds and every business rule live in one place, and every decision is stamped with its version.

::: {.keyidea}
Everything that can change a decision lives in one place, with a version number.
:::

**A record for every decision.** A decision model gives probabilities, not reasons. But record the raw and calibrated probabilities, the thresholds they met, the rule that fired and the version that decided, and every *action* becomes explainable, even though the model explains nothing.

![One decision record, with notes on why each field is there. Together they say what the service saw, what the model said, what the policy did, which version decided, and why.](/figures/ch28/record.pdf){#fig-record}

**Fitted together.** A dry run over a live week flagged day one: the queue was over capacity. The thresholds had been fitted for 240 reviews a day, and *afterwards* someone added a sensible rule, never auto-close an alert on a critical system. Every alert it moved to review was work the thresholds hadn't allowed for. Fitted *with* the rule, the queue fit again, from about {{< num ch28 v1_mean_reviews int >}} a day to {{< num ch28 v2_mean_reviews int >}}.

![Alerts sent to review each day of the live week, before and after the fix. Fitted without the critical-asset rule, the thresholds let the queue run over capacity every day. Fitted with it, the act threshold rises slightly and the queue fits.](/figures/ch28/dry-run.pdf){#fig-dry-run}

::: {.keyidea}
Thresholds and business rules are one decision, and they have to be fitted together.
:::

**A monitor, an owner, and shadow mode.** Once a day, check the share of cases in each door, the queue against capacity, the fallback rate, and predicted against confirmed threats. On a campaign's first day, two flags go up, and the second, *predicted real far below confirmed real*, says in plain numbers that the probabilities are no longer calibrated. A named owner can switch the service to "review everything" while they find out why. And every improvement runs in shadow beside the current version first: here, the candidate agreed on {{< num ch28 shadow_agree pct >}} of alerts, and the shadow run measured, before anyone paid it, the threats its changes would let through.

![Two weeks of the daily monitor: the live week, then the phishing campaign. Top: the review queue, red and striped on days a flag was raised. Bottom: for alerts people saw, the share the model predicted to be real against the share they confirmed. The campaign opens a gap on its first day.](/figures/ch28/monitor.pdf){#fig-monitor}

## Build your own System One model

You don't need to build one to use one. But building a small one shows what its probabilities are made of.

![The three heads. A noul turns one number into P(yes) with the S-curve. A choice turns one number per label into probabilities that add up to 1. A score turns one number into probabilities for levels in order, by cutting it at points that must stay in order.](/figures/ch27/heads.pdf){#fig-heads}

The design follows the interface. A shared **encoder** reads an alert once and turns it into 32 numbers. Three small **heads** read those numbers, one per question type (@fig-heads). Yes/no uses Chapter 2's S-curve. Pick-one uses a softmax, so the probabilities add to 1. Rate-on-a-scale uses one "dial" cut at ordered points, so that "high" stays above "medium". All three are trained together with log loss, which rewards honest probabilities (Chapter 2), then a temperature per head is fitted on held-back data (Chapter 3). The whole model has {{< num ch27 n_params int >}} numbers and trains in seconds.

Calibration error on a fresh week fell from {{< num ch27 raw_ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch27 temp_ece f3 >}} after the temperature, with ranking unchanged. A deliberately oversized, overtrained version was the warning: its calibration error was {{< num ch27 over_ece f3 >}}, and after a temperature it was no better, {{< num ch27 over_ece_temp f3 >}}. A correction can soften answers; it can't restore what memorising destroyed.

![Reliability of P(attack) on the live week. Left: TinyJev as trained, slightly overconfident. Middle: after dividing by the fitted temperature. Right: the overtrained network before any temperature; its problems are ones no single temperature can fix.](/figures/ch27/calibration.pdf){#fig-calibration}

::: {.keyidea}
Train with a proper scoring rule, stop before the model memorises, then calibrate on data it has never seen.
:::

::: {.breaks}
This is a teaching design. A real service also needs authentication, rate limits, a proper log store, access control on the configuration, and protection for personal data in what it records. Shadow comparisons only show where versions *disagree*; if both are wrong the same way, keep the random audit going. And the small model reads structured fields from one company; it will drift as soon as the world changes.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. For a service you rely on, list three errors you'd retry and three you'd fix. What should a failed call *mean* for each decision it makes?
:::

Next: what changes, for the industry and for you, when deciding becomes cheap, fast and calibrated.
